# Introduction

`flight_recorder` is a small library for logging what a robot's control node *computes*, from inside the node,
at control rate, without disturbing the control loop. It has two writers (Python and header-only C++) that produce
the **same HDF5 file layout**, and a Python reader that loads that layout into pandas.

This guide explains the whole package. It covers why it exists, the on-disk format, the memory and threading model
behind the fast append, how incremental flushing makes it crash-tolerant, every public Python and C++ API, the ROS 2
patterns, the command line, the ROS2Logger compatibility layer, the benchmarks, the tests, and the limitations.
Everything below matches version **0.1.2** of the code and **format version 1**. All figures were generated by
`docs/guide/make_figures.py` from the real library.

The whole API in three snippets (from the README):

```python
from flight_recorder import Recorder

rec = Recorder('flight.h5', metadata={'robot': 'skie_2'}, autosave_period=5.0)
ticks = rec.stream('ticks', ['time', 'x', 'y', 'z', 'yaw', 'thrust'])   # once, at init

ticks.append(t, x, y, z, yaw, thrust)                                    # every tick
rec.record('plans', seq, {'tube': tube, 'ref': ref}, {'t_start': t})     # big arrays: only when they change
rec.event(t, 'backup', 'no certified plan')                              # rare, timestamped strings

rec.save()                                                               # at shutdown (final flush)
```

```cpp
#include <flight_recorder/recorder.hpp>

fr::Recorder rec("flight.h5", {{"robot", std::string("skie_2")}});
auto& ticks = rec.stream("ticks", {"time", "x", "y", "z", "yaw", "thrust"});
ticks.append(t, x, y, z, yaw, thrust);                                   // ~15 ns
rec.record("plans", seq, {{"tube", fr::Array(tube.data(), {rows, 10})}}, {{"t_start", t}});
rec.save();
```

```python
from flight_recorder import FlightLog

with FlightLog('flight.h5') as log:
    df = log['ticks']                          # pandas DataFrame
    tube = log.record('plans', 12)['tube']     # a stored array
    print(log.summary())
```

**How to read this guide.** If you only want to use the library, read sections [-@sec-data-model],
[-@sec-python-api], [-@sec-ros2] and [-@sec-limitations]. For the file format read section [-@sec-format]. For why
it is fast and safe, read sections [-@sec-memory] and [-@sec-flush]. The shorter repository documents are
complementary:
[`docs/DESIGN.md`](../DESIGN.md) (design notes), [`docs/COMPARISON.md`](../COMPARISON.md) (against other logging
methods) and [`docs/MIGRATION.md`](../MIGRATION.md) (moving from ROS2Logger).

# Why a dedicated flight logger? {#sec-why}

Research control nodes usually log by appending to Python lists: ROS2Logger's `LogType`s, a list of rows, or a list
of dicts. They then write a CSV at shutdown. In a 100 Hz controller that has three costs that are easy to miss.

**1. Garbage-collector stalls.** CPython frees most objects by reference counting. Container objects (lists, dicts,
tuples, class instances) are *also* tracked by a cyclic garbage collector that periodically scans them looking for
reference cycles. The collector is generational. A *full* collection scans every tracked object in the process and
holds the GIL while it runs, so every Python thread freezes, including the control loop. Full collections become
both slower and more frequent as long-lived tracked objects accumulate: CPython triggers one when that population has
grown by 25 %. A logger that keeps one list per tick feeds exactly this. In the RTA-MM-GPR node that motivated the
library, logging lists were about 97 % of the tracked objects at the end of a flight. Full collections took
**≈300 ms each, 4–5 times per flight**, which is 30 missed control ticks each time.

**2. Memory.** A Python `float` is a 24-byte object, plus an 8-byte pointer in the list that holds it. A list of
floats therefore costs about 4× the data, and nested lists of rows more. In the benchmark (section
[-@sec-bench]), ROS2Logger holds 42 MB for 4.8 MB of numbers.

**3. Nothing reaches the disk until shutdown.** A crash, `kill -9`, a failed `destroy_node()` or a power loss loses
the whole flight.

`flight_recorder` removes all three:

* each stream lives in **one preallocated float64 array**. `append` copies the numbers into it and keeps no Python
  objects, so the collector never sees the data ([@fig-gc]);
* large arrays that change rarely (plans, trajectories, gain matrices) are **stored once, when they change**, instead
  of being re-logged every tick;
* everything goes to **one self-describing HDF5 file** that is **flushed incrementally**. With
  `autosave_period=5.0`, a crash loses at most 5 s.

![New objects the cyclic GC must track while logging 60 000 ticks of 4 values. The list-based logger adds one
tracked list per tick. The flight_recorder stream, which also grows by doubling from 1024 rows, adds a handful
(4 in this run). Measured with `gc.get_objects()` while the GC was disabled.](figures/gc_tracked.pdf){#fig-gc
width=85%}

# Architecture and data model {#sec-data-model}

## The pieces

![Package architecture. Three kinds of writer produce one file format. The Python reader, the CLI and any HDF5
tool read it.](figures/architecture.pdf){#fig-arch width=100%}

| file | role |
|---|---|
| `flight_recorder/format.py` | the normative constants: names of the three groups, `FORMAT_VERSION = 1`, `CHUNK_ROWS = 4096`, `GZIP_LEVEL = 4` |
| `flight_recorder/buffer.py` | `ColumnBuffer`: the append-only float64 table behind every Python stream |
| `flight_recorder/recorder.py` | `Recorder` (collect + flush), `record_key`, `git_commit` |
| `flight_recorder/reader.py` | `FlightLog`: read either writer's files into DataFrames and arrays |
| `flight_recorder/csv_export.py` | plain CSV and ROS2Logger-layout CSV export |
| `flight_recorder/compat.py` | ROS2Logger-compatible `Logger`, `LogType`, `VectorLogType`, `install_shutdown_logging` |
| `flight_recorder/__main__.py`, `scripts/flight_recorder` | command line (`info`, `csv`, `ros2logger-csv`) |
| `include/flight_recorder/recorder.hpp` | header-only C++ writer (`fr::Recorder`, `fr::Stream`, `fr::Array`) on the HDF5 C API |
| `examples/`, `benchmarks/`, `test/` | a ROS 2 node, a C++ program, the benchmark harness, 17 tests |

: Repository map. {#tbl-files tbl-colwidths="[47,53]"}

The package builds with colcon as an `ament_cmake` package. It installs the Python module, the `flight_recorder`
script, the header, and the CMake target `flight_recorder::flight_recorder`. Outside ROS, `pip install -e .`
installs the Python part (`pyproject.toml`; dependencies `numpy`, `h5py`, `pandas`).

## Four kinds of data

A flight produces data of different shapes at different rates, and each is stored the way it is produced:

| kind | example | API | stored as |
|---|---|---|---|
| **stream** | time, state, commands, timings: fixed columns, one row per tick | `rec.stream(name, columns)`, then `.append(...)` | one float64 dataset per column |
| **record** | a plan, a trajectory, a gain matrix: arrays that change rarely | `rec.record(group, key, arrays, attrs)` | one HDF5 group per record |
| **event** | "backup engaged", a mode switch: rare, timestamped strings | `rec.event(t, kind, detail)` | three parallel datasets |
| **metadata** | robot, parameters, git commit, host, date | `Recorder(metadata=...)`, `set_metadata(...)` | root attributes |

: The data model. {#tbl-model tbl-colwidths="[12,34,30,24]"}

The stream/record split is the main design idea. The RTA node that motivated the library logged a 12 × 4 slice of its
reachable tube *on every control tick*, because a per-tick table was the only shape its logger had. The tube only
changed when a new plan arrived, about 1 tick in 30. With records, each plan is stored **once, in full**, and each
tick stores only the plan number (and row) it used. On a real flight that was 5.42 MB → 1.61 MB, while also keeping
more information: the full tube instead of a slice.

**Streams** are declared once with fixed column names. Use one stream per *rate or producer* (control ticks at
100 Hz, an estimator at 10 Hz, …) instead of one wide table. Align them afterwards with `pandas.merge_asof`
(section [-@sec-analysis]).

# The file format (version 1) {#sec-format}

## Layout

```text
flight.h5
├── attrs: format="flight_recorder", format_version=1, writer="python"|"cpp",
│          created (ISO 8601, local time, seconds), host, <user metadata>
├── streams/
│   └── <stream>/              attrs: columns = [names, in order], n_rows
│       └── <column>           float64 (n_rows,), chunks of 4096 rows, shuffle + gzip 4, resizable
├── records/
│   └── <group>/
│       └── <key>/             attrs: the attrs given to record(...)
│           └── <name>         float64 array of any shape (shuffle + gzip above 256 elements)
└── events/
    ├── time                   float64 (n,)        chunks of 256, resizable, uncompressed
    ├── kind                   UTF-8 string (n,)   chunks of 256, resizable, uncompressed
    └── detail                 UTF-8 string (n,)   chunks of 256, resizable, uncompressed
```

This is the layout `flight_recorder/format.py` documents, and both writers produce it. Below is the actual layout of
the synthetic 60 s flight that `make_figures.py` records with the Python writer. It is walked with `h5py`, and only 2
of the 40 plan records are shown:

{{< include figures/format_tree.md >}}

## Streams

* **Column-major on disk.** Each column is its own 1-D dataset. Reading one signal (`log.column('ticks', 'z')`)
  touches only that dataset, and building a DataFrame needs no reshuffling.
* **Order and length live in attributes.** The group attribute `columns` holds the names in declaration order.
  HDF5 lists members alphabetically, so the reader always uses this attribute. `n_rows` is the number of rows
  written so far, updated on every flush.
* **Chunked, resizable, compressed.** Every column is created with `maxshape=(None,)`, `chunks=(4096,)`
  (32 KiB of float64 per chunk), the **shuffle** filter and **gzip**. The level is `compression_level`, 4 by
  default. The shuffle filter regroups the bytes of consecutive values: all first bytes together, then all second
  bytes, and so on. For smooth signals the high-order bytes (sign, exponent, leading mantissa) repeat, and gzip then
  compresses them well.
* **Everything is float64.** Integers and booleans are exact up to 2^53^. Missing values are `NaN`.

![File size of one 30 000 × 20 stream against the gzip level, for flight-like smooth signals (with a small noise
floor) and for random normal data, compared with raw float64 and with CSV written at full precision. Level 0 is
*larger* than raw: with nothing compressed, the last, partly filled 4096-row chunk of each column is stored whole
(32 768 rows of storage for 30 000). Most of the gain comes at level 1, and the
default of 4 is on the plateau. On real flight data the effect is larger: 0.36 MB against 1.28 MB of CSV for a
2000 × 34 table (README).](figures/compression.pdf){#fig-compression width=100%}

## Records

* Stored under `records/<group>/<key>/`, one group per record, one dataset per array. Arrays can have any shape
  (converted to float64).
* **Integer keys are zero-padded to six digits** (`record_key(12) == '000012'`; C++ uses `%06lld`). HDF5 iterates
  alphabetically, so the padding makes that order numeric. String keys are used as they are.
* Arrays with **more than 256 elements** get shuffle + gzip. Smaller ones are stored contiguously, where the filter
  overhead is not worth it. (Python lets h5py pick the chunk shape; C++ uses one chunk of the array's full shape.)
* **Re-recording a key replaces it.** The flush deletes the old group before writing the new one
  (`test_rerecording_a_key_replaces_it`).
* Record attributes accept scalars, strings and small arrays. The conversion rules are in
  @tbl-attrs.

| Python value | stored as |
|---|---|
| `bool` / `numpy.bool_` | integer 0/1 |
| `str`, `int`, `float`, NumPy scalar | as is |
| `list` / `tuple` / `ndarray` of numbers or bools | float64 array |
| `list` / `tuple` / `ndarray` of anything else | array of UTF-8 strings |
| `None` | skipped (not written) |
| anything else | `str(value)` |

: How Python metadata and record attributes are written (`recorder._attr_value`). C++ attribute values are a
`std::variant<double, int64_t, std::string, std::vector<double>>`. {#tbl-attrs tbl-colwidths="[50,50]"}

## Events

Three parallel 1-D datasets. `time` is float64, and `kind` and `detail` are variable-length UTF-8 strings. All three
are resizable with chunks of 256 and uncompressed, and a flush appends to all three together. The `events` group and
its datasets exist even if no event was ever logged (length 0).

## Root metadata

The writer always sets `format`, `format_version`, `writer` (`"python"` or `"cpp"`), `created` (local time, ISO 8601
to the second) and `host`. User metadata is merged on top. In Python, `Recorder(metadata=...)` is applied *after* the
defaults, so it can override them, e.g. `host`. Metadata is rewritten on every flush, so `set_metadata` late in the
flight still reaches the file.

## Reading without this library

The file is plain HDF5. It can be read with `h5ls -r flight.h5`, `h5dump`, HDFView, MATLAB `h5read`, Julia
`HDF5.jl`, or `h5py` alone:

```python
import h5py, numpy as np
with h5py.File('flight.h5', 'r') as f:
    g = f['streams/ticks']
    cols = [c.decode() if isinstance(c, bytes) else c for c in g.attrs['columns']]
    data = {c: g[c][()] for c in cols}                     # dict of float64 arrays
    plan = f['records/plans/000012/tube'][()]
```

**Compatibility.** `FlightLog` accepts files whose root attribute `format` equals `"flight_recorder"` and whose
`format_version` is at most the one it supports (1). A file from a newer writer raises a `ValueError` that names both
versions, instead of being misread. `test_cpp_roundtrip.py` checks that the C++ writer's
output reads back bit-exactly with the Python reader.

# Memory model: why `append` is cheap {#sec-memory}

![The two stream buffers. Left: Python keeps one NumPy array per stream and doubles it when full. Right: C++ keeps a
fixed table of pointers to 4096-row blocks that never move.](figures/memory_model.pdf){#fig-memory width=100%}

## Python: `ColumnBuffer`

A `ColumnBuffer` is `(capacity × columns)` float64, initialised to `NaN`, plus a row counter `_n`:

```python
def append(self, *values):
    if self._n == self._data.shape[0]:
        self._grow()                  # new array of 2x rows, copy the _n valid rows, swap
    self._data[self._n] = values      # the numbers are copied into the array
    self._n += 1                      # published AFTER the row is written
```

* **No per-row objects survive.** The argument tuple and the float objects are freed by reference counting as soon
  as `append` returns. Nothing is added to what the cyclic GC tracks; `test_gc.py` asserts fewer than 100 new tracked
  objects over 100 000 appends ([@fig-gc]).
* **Growth by doubling** (amortised O(1)). Pass `capacity=` ≈ the flight length to never grow in flight: 100 Hz ×
  600 s = 60 000 rows, which is 480 KB per column. `Recorder.stream` defaults to 4096 rows; a bare `ColumnBuffer`
  defaults to 1024.
* **Two hot-path forms.** `append(*values)` unpacks arguments. `append_array(row)` takes a sequence or array that
  is already built, and is about twice as fast for wide rows (@tbl-measured).
* The row width is checked by NumPy: a wrong number of values raises `ValueError` (`test_rejects_wrong_row_width`).
* Readers: `column(name)` returns a **view** of the valid rows; `rows(start, stop)`, `as_dict()` and
  `to_dataframe()` return copies.

{{< include figures/measured.md >}}

![Distribution of the per-tick hot-path cost for 20 values, on the machine that built this guide (best of 3 runs of
30 000 ticks). A bare `list.append` is cheaper *in the loop*: that is why list-based logging looks free. It pays
later, in GC scans and memory. The compat layer calls 20 separate `LogType.append`s, one per logged
variable.](figures/append_latency.pdf){#fig-latency width=100%}

Absolute numbers depend on the machine and its load. The benchmark in section [-@sec-bench] measures `append_array`
at 0.52 µs p50 / 1.6 µs p99 in a clean, isolated process.

## C++: `fr::Stream`

```cpp
template <typename... Ts> void append(Ts... values);   // static_cast<double> each, then append_row
void append_row(const double* row, size_t count) {
  const size_t n = n_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
  double* dst = ensure_block(n / kBlockRows) + (n % kBlockRows) * width_;
  for (size_t i = 0; i < width_; ++i) dst[i] = row[i];
  n_.store(n + 1, std::memory_order_release);          // publish the complete row
}
```

* Rows live in **blocks of `kBlockRows = 4096` rows** (row-major). A fixed table of `kMaxBlocks = 65 536` block
  pointers is allocated when the stream is created, so a stream holds at most ≈268 M rows (`std::length_error`
  beyond that). The table itself is 512 KiB of pointers.
* Blocks are **never moved or freed** while the recorder exists, unlike a `std::vector`, which reallocates as it
  grows. That is what makes a concurrent flush safe (section [-@sec-threads]).
* The constructor preallocates enough blocks for `capacity` rows (default 4096). Beyond that one block is allocated
  every 4096 rows, the only allocation on the hot path.
* A wrong number of values throws `std::invalid_argument`.
* Cost: **≈15 ns per append** (`cpp_bench`: 0.016 µs p50 and 2.2 µs p99 when rebuilt for this guide; the p99 is the
  one tick in 50 that also copies a 100 × 10 plan into `record`).

# Threading {#sec-threads}

The rules are the same in both languages:

* **One writer thread per stream**, normally the control loop. Different streams may be written by different
  threads.
* **`flush()` may run on any other thread at the same time.** Only one flush runs at a time; a second one waits for
  the flush lock.
* `record()`, `event()` (and, in C++, `set_metadata()`) take a short mutex. They are meant for rare data, not for
  every tick.

Why a concurrent flush only reads complete rows:

* **Python.** `_n` is incremented after the row is written, and under the GIL the flusher sees those two steps in
  that order. `rows(start)` reads `_n` once and copies the rows below it. If the writer grows the buffer during a
  flush, the flusher still holds the old array, whose first `_n` rows are complete.
* **C++.** The writer stores `n_` with `memory_order_release` after writing the row. The flusher loads it with
  `memory_order_acquire` (`size()`), so every row below it is visible. Blocks never move, so a pointer to an old
  block stays valid.

Both are tested under stress. In Python, 50 000 appends run while another thread flushes in a tight loop, and every
value is checked. In C++, `cpp_example --concurrent-flush` flushes every 2 ms while writing 20 000 rows, and
`test_cpp_roundtrip.py` checks every value.

# Incremental flushing and crash tolerance {#sec-flush}

## What a flush does

```text
flush():
  take the flush lock
  snapshot (under the data lock): the stream list, records and events not yet flushed
  open the file: mode "w" on the first flush (replaces any old file), "a" afterwards
  write all metadata attributes
  for each stream: new rows = rows [flushed_rows, n) -> resize every column dataset, write the new rows,
                   flushed_rows = n, attrs n_rows = n
  write the new records (replacing existing keys) and append the new events
  close the file
```

Every flush **closes the file**, and `save()` is simply the last flush. Two consequences:

* **Between flushes the file is closed and consistent.** It can be opened with `FlightLog` while the node is still
  flying, e.g. for a live plot every few seconds (`test_autosave_writes_periodically` does exactly this).
* **A crash loses only what was not flushed yet.** `test_crash_after_flush_keeps_flushed_data` runs a process that
  flushes 1000 rows, appends 1000 more and dies with `os._exit(1)` (no `save()`, no `atexit`, no `finally`). The file
  contains exactly the first 1000.

`test_incremental_flush_equals_single_save` checks that many small flushes produce the same data as one save.

![Rows appended by a writer at about 1 kHz (sleeping between ticks, like an rclpy timer) against rows safely on disk
with `autosave_period=0.5`. The flushes happen on the recorder's background thread. If the process died at the red
line, everything below the green staircase would survive.](figures/incremental_flush.pdf){#fig-flush width=90%}

## Autosave (Python)

`Recorder(path, autosave_period=5.0)` starts a daemon thread named `flight_recorder_autosave` that calls `flush()`
every period. If the path is only known later (common in ROS nodes, where the path depends on parameters or on the
log directory), create the recorder without one and call `rec.start_autosave(period, path)` once it is known
(`test_start_autosave_later`). The autosave thread never raises into the host process: a failed flush prints
`[flight_recorder] autosave failed: …` and the thread tries again next period. `save()` stops the thread, joins it
(5 s timeout) and does the final flush. `start_autosave` may be called again after `save()` to keep recording into
the same file.

**Final flush at exit.** Once a recorder has written its file (first flush), an `atexit` hook, which holds only a
weak reference, calls `save()` at interpreter exit if the recorder still exists. Rows appended after the last autosave
are therefore not lost when a node forgets `save()` or exits normally. A crash or `kill -9` still loses up to one
autosave period.

**C++** has no autosave thread. Call `rec.flush()` periodically, e.g. from a 1 Hz ROS timer in its own callback
group, so that it runs concurrently with the control timer. `~fr::Recorder()` does a final flush when the recorder
has a path.

## Caveats

* **HDF5 is not a journaling format.** A crash *during* a flush can leave the file unreadable. Flushes are short
  (milliseconds for a few seconds of data). If that risk matters, copy the file after each flush, or also record the
  raw topics with rosbag2/MCAP.
* **Flush cost is mostly gzip.** Compressing and writing 30 000 × 20 values plus 600 plans in one go takes about
  250 ms (Python) or 160 ms (C++). A periodic flush costs proportionally less.
* **In Python, flushes compete with the control loop for the GIL.** h5py holds the GIL while it compresses and
  writes, so prefer frequent, small flushes to rare, big ones.
* **Autosave keeps up even with a busy-waiting writer.** CPython hands the GIL to a waiting thread every 5 ms
  (`sys.getswitchinterval()`), so the autosave thread runs even if the control loop never blocks. Measured: a
  100 Hz loop that busy-waits between ticks had 217 of 220 rows on disk after 2.2 s (autosave period 0.2 s), and a
  loop appending as fast as possible had 4.37 M of 5.27 M rows on disk. (An earlier draft of this guide claimed the
  opposite; that measurement did not reproduce.)

# Python API {#sec-python-api}

## `Recorder`

```python
Recorder(path=None, metadata=None, autosave_period=None, compression_level=4)
```

| member | what it does |
|---|---|
| `stream(name, columns, capacity=4096) -> ColumnBuffer` | declare a stream once, at init; keep the returned buffer. Duplicate names and empty or duplicate columns raise `ValueError` |
| `rec[name]` | the `ColumnBuffer` of an existing stream |
| `record(group, key, arrays, attrs=None, copy=False)` | store rarely changing arrays **once** under `records/<group>/<key>`. The arrays are converted with `np.asarray(..., float)` and **kept by reference until the next flush**: pass data you won't modify, or `copy=True`. An array and an attribute with the same name raise `ValueError` |
| `event(t, kind, detail='')` | a timestamped string pair |
| `set_metadata(**values)` | add or replace root attributes (written at every flush) |
| `flush(path=None) -> str` | append everything new to the file; safe from another thread. Returns the path |
| `save(path=None) -> str` | stop autosave, then do a final flush |
| `start_autosave(period, path=None)` | start the background flush thread (again after `save()` if needed) |
| context manager | `with Recorder(path) as rec: ...` calls `save()` on exit if a path is set |

: `Recorder` API (`flight_recorder/recorder.py`). {#tbl-recorder tbl-colwidths="[40,60]"}

Rules worth knowing:

* **One recorder writes one file.** After the first flush, flushing to a different path raises
  `ValueError('already writing …; a recorder writes one file')`. Later flushes append only the new rows at their
  offsets, so another file would miss the earlier ones.
* **HDF5 extensions are kept; anything else gets `.h5` appended.** `run.h5`, `run.hdf5`, `run.hdf` and `run.he5`
  are used as given; `run` becomes `run.h5` and `run.csv` becomes `run.csv.h5` (nothing is silently dropped). C++
  uses the same rule. The returned path, and `rec.path` afterwards, are the real one.
* **The first flush replaces an existing file** at that path (mode `"w"`).

Helpers: `record_key(key)` gives the zero-padded key string, and `git_commit(path)` gives the short hash of the git
repository containing `path`, or `''`. It is handy as metadata: `metadata={'git_commit': git_commit(__file__)}`.

## `ColumnBuffer`

Returned by `rec.stream(...)`: `append(*values)`, `append_array(row)`, `len(buf)`, `buf.width`, `buf.columns`,
`column(name)` (a view), `rows(start=0, stop=None)`, `as_dict()` and `to_dataframe()` (copies). Section
[-@sec-memory] explains its internals.

## `FlightLog`

```python
with FlightLog('flight.h5') as log:
    log.metadata                  # dict of root attributes (bytes decoded, NumPy scalars as Python values)
    log.streams                   # ['estimator', 'ticks']
    log.columns('ticks')          # names in declaration order
    x = log.column('ticks', 'x')  # one column, without reading the others
    df = log['ticks']             # == log.stream('ticks'): pandas DataFrame
    log.record_groups             # ['plans']
    log.record_keys('plans')      # ['000000', '000001', ...] (sorted)
    p = log.record('plans', 12)   # {'reference': array, 't_start': 18.0, 'horizon_s': 3.0}
    log.events                    # DataFrame(time, kind, detail)
    print(log.summary())
```

`record(group, key)` returns **one dict** that merges the arrays *and* the attributes, so an attribute with the same
name as an array overwrites it in the dict. `FlightLog` opens the file read-only and raises `ValueError` if the
`format` attribute is not `"flight_recorder"`. For the synthetic flight, `summary()` prints:

{{< include figures/summary.md >}}

## A complete example

This is, in short, what `make_figures.py` does to produce [@fig-flight]: a 100 Hz "ticks" stream, a second 10 Hz
stream, a plan recorded every 1.5 s with the plan number logged per tick, three events, and a flush every 5 s of
flight.

```python
import numpy as np
from flight_recorder import Recorder, FlightLog

rec = Recorder('synthetic_flight.h5',
               metadata={'robot': 'skie_2', 'rate_hz': 100.0, 'gains': [6.0, 4.5, 1.0]})
ticks = rec.stream('ticks', ['time', 'x', 'y', 'z', 'x_ref', 'y_ref', 'z_ref', 'thrust', 'plan_seq'],
                   capacity=6000)
est = rec.stream('estimator', ['time', 'bias_x', 'bias_y'], capacity=600)
seq = -1
for k in range(6000):
    t = 0.01 * k
    ...                                                   # state estimate, reference, control
    if k % 150 == 0:                                      # a new plan: stored ONCE, in full
        seq += 1
        rec.record('plans', seq, {'reference': plan}, {'t_start': t, 'horizon_s': 3.0})
    ticks.append(t, *pos, *ref, thrust, seq)              # per tick: numbers only (+ which plan)
    if k % 10 == 0:
        est.append(t, bx, by)
    if k == 3100:
        rec.event(t, 'mode', 'gust detected')
    if k % 500 == 499:
        rec.flush()                                       # or autosave_period=5.0
rec.save()
```

![The synthetic flight read back with `FlightLog`. The tick stream (blue) with its reference (green), every fourth
stored plan (orange, from `records/plans/*/reference`), the events as dashed lines, and a second stream at 10 Hz
next to the per-tick `plan_seq` column.](figures/synthetic_flight.pdf){#fig-flight width=100%}

## Analysis recipes {#sec-analysis}

```python
import pandas as pd
from flight_recorder import FlightLog

with FlightLog('run.h5') as log:
    ticks, est = log['ticks'], log['estimator']
    merged = pd.merge_asof(ticks, est, on='time')                # streams at different rates, aligned
    plan = log.record('plans', int(ticks['plan_seq'].iloc[500])) # the plan active at tick 500
    ev = log.events[log.events['kind'] == 'mode']                # filter events
    ticks.to_parquet('run_ticks.parquet')                         # hand off to an analysis pipeline
```

# C++ API {#sec-cpp}

`include/flight_recorder/recorder.hpp` is header-only and uses the HDF5 **C** API directly: no HDF5 C++ bindings, no
HighFive. Its only dependency is `libhdf5-dev`. Everything is in namespace `fr`.

| item | details |
|---|---|
| `fr::Recorder(std::string path = "", const Attributes& metadata = {})` | sets `format`, `format_version`, `writer="cpp"`, `created`, `host`, then your metadata |
| `Stream& stream(name, columns, capacity = 4096)` | the reference stays valid for the recorder's lifetime; a duplicate name throws `std::invalid_argument` |
| `stream.append(v...)` / `append_row(const double*, size_t)` | hot path; the number of values must equal the number of columns |
| `~Recorder()` | final flush if a path is set (errors are printed to stderr, never thrown) |
| `record(group, std::string key, std::map<std::string, Array>, Attributes = {})` | string keys are used as they are |
| `record(group, int64_t key, ...)` | integer keys zero-padded to 6 digits |
| `event(double t, kind, detail = "")`, `set_metadata(key, Value)` | under the data mutex |
| `std::string flush(const std::string& path = "")` | append everything new; may run on another thread; one file per recorder |
| `std::string save(const std::string& path = "")` | the same as `flush` (the final one) |
| `fr::Array(const double* data, {dims...})`, `fr::Array(std::vector<double>, {dims...})` | a row-major N-d array; **copies** the data. An empty shape `{}` is a scalar. The vector form throws `std::invalid_argument` if the size does not match the shape |
| `fr::Value` | `std::variant<double, int64_t, std::string, std::vector<double>>` |
| `fr::Attributes` | `std::vector<std::pair<std::string, Value>>` |

: The C++ writer (`fr` namespace). {#tbl-cpp tbl-colwidths="[48,52]"}

**Errors.** Every failed HDF5 call throws `std::runtime_error("flight_recorder: HDF5 call failed: <function>")`.
While `flush()` runs, HDF5's automatic error printing is switched off (so problems arrive only as exceptions), and the
previous handler is restored afterwards (RAII `detail::QuietHdf5Errors`). Other HDF5 users in the process keep their
error reporting. A failed flush puts the unwritten records and events back, so a later flush retries them.

**Save on destruction.** `~fr::Recorder()` does a final flush if the recorder has a path, and prints (never throws)
any error. Still call `flush()` periodically for crash tolerance.

**Using it from CMake / colcon:**

```cmake
find_package(flight_recorder REQUIRED)
target_link_libraries(my_node flight_recorder::flight_recorder)   # include paths + HDF5 C link line
```

and `<depend>flight_recorder</depend>` in `package.xml`. The package also builds two programs:
`cpp_example <out.h5> [rows] [--concurrent-flush]` (the fixture of the C++ round-trip test) and
`cpp_bench <out.h5> [ticks]`.

**In a ROS 2 C++ node** (from `docs/MIGRATION.md`):

```cpp
#include <flight_recorder/recorder.hpp>
fr::Recorder rec_{path, {{"node", std::string("offboard")}}};
fr::Stream& ticks_ = rec_.stream("ticks", {"time", "x", "y", "z", "yaw"}, 60000);
// control timer:                    ticks_.append(t, x, y, z, yaw);
// 1 Hz timer in its own callback group: rec_.flush();
// shutdown:                         rec_.save();
```

# ROS 2 integration {#sec-ros2}

`examples/ros2_node_example.py` shows the pattern for any control node:

1. **Declare the streams once in `__init__`**, with fixed float64 columns and `capacity` ≈ the flight length.
2. **One `append` per tick** in the control callback, numbers only.
3. **`record` large arrays only when they change**, and put their sequence number in the tick stream.
4. **`save()` at shutdown**, in `main`'s `finally`. `autosave_period` keeps a crash from losing more than a few
   seconds.

```python
class ExampleController(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('flight_recorder_example')
        self.rec = Recorder('example_flight.h5', autosave_period=5.0,
                            metadata={'node': self.get_name(), 'git_commit': git_commit(__file__),
                                      'rate_hz': 100.0})
        self.ticks = self.rec.stream('ticks', ['time', 'x', 'y', 'z', 'yaw', 'u_thrust', 'comp_time'],
                                     capacity=60_000)
        self.create_timer(0.01, self.control)

    def control(self):
        ...
        self.ticks.append(t, x, y, z, yaw, u, time.perf_counter() - c0)

def main():
    rclpy.init(); node = ExampleController()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    finally:
        print(node.rec.save())
        node.destroy_node()
```

Practical points:

* **Where to write.** Use one file per node and per run. HDF5 file locking refuses a second writer on the same file.
  If the path comes from a parameter, use `start_autosave(period, path)` once you know it.
* **Metadata is free.** Put the parameters, gains, git commit and controller mode in `metadata=`, so the file
  describes itself.
* **Pair it with rosbag2.** `flight_recorder` records what a node computes, from inside it. rosbag2/MCAP records
  what flows on topics between nodes, and can replay it. They are complementary: see `docs/COMPARISON.md`.

# Command line and CSV export {#sec-cli}

```bash
python3 -m flight_recorder info flight.h5                        # summary(): streams, records, events, metadata
python3 -m flight_recorder csv flight.h5 ticks -o ticks.csv      # plain CSV of one stream
python3 -m flight_recorder ros2logger-csv flight.h5 ticks -o legacy.csv
ros2 run flight_recorder flight_recorder info flight.h5          # the same, through the installed script
```

Without `-o`, the output is `<file>_<stream>.csv` next to the input. The functions behind the CLI are in
`flight_recorder.csv_export`:

* `stream_to_csv(log, stream, path)`: `DataFrame.to_csv(index=False, na_rep='nan')`;
* `stream_to_ros2logger_csv(log, stream, path, required=REQUIRED)`: one stream in ROS2Logger's layout;
* `write_ros2logger_csv(columns, path, required=REQUIRED) -> (rows, cols)`: the general writer. It takes
  `(header, values, order, tie_key)` tuples and orders the columns with the required ones first
  (`REQUIRED = ('time', 'x', 'y', 'z', 'yaw')`), then by `(order, tie_key, header)`. Shorter columns are padded
  with `NaN`, and values are written by Python's `csv` module (floats as `repr`, NaN as `nan`), exactly like
  ROS2Logger. A missing required column raises `ValueError('[flight_recorder] Missing required logs: [...]')`.

# ROS2Logger compatibility and migration {#sec-compat}

`flight_recorder.compat` is a drop-in replacement for ROS2Logger's API. Change one import:

```python
# from ros2_logger import Logger, LogType, VectorLogType, install_shutdown_logging
from flight_recorder.compat import Logger, LogType, VectorLogType, install_shutdown_logging
```

| class / function | behaviour |
|---|---|
| `LogType(name, order, capacity=4096)` | scalar log: `append(value)`, `extend(values)`, `.data` (a copy), `len()` |
| `VectorLogType(name, order, subnames, capacity=4096)` | one column per sub-name: `append(*values)` (checks the count), `append_dict(**kw)`; CSV headers `<name>_<subname>` |
| `Logger(filename, base_dir, required=REQUIRED, write_h5=True)` | ROS2Logger's path convention `…/src/data_analysis/log_files/<pkg>/<filename>` (`build`/`install` mapped to `src`) |
| `Logger.log(source)` | finds every `LogType`/`VectorLogType` attribute of `source` (via `vars()`), writes the byte-identical CSV, and, if `write_h5`, an `.h5` next to it with **one stream per log** (sharing the buffers, not copying them) |
| `install_shutdown_logging(logger, source, *, also_shutdown=None, include_atexit=True)` | logs once on SIGINT/SIGTERM (and at exit), then `destroy_node()` and `rclpy.shutdown()` or your `also_shutdown` |

: The compat layer (`flight_recorder/compat.py`). {#tbl-compat tbl-colwidths="[42,58]"}

The values live in `ColumnBuffer`s, so the compat logs add nothing to the GC's work (`test_gc.py`). The
differences from ROS2Logger: values must be numeric, and ROS2Logger's analysis notebooks are not copied into the log
directory. `test_compat.py` compares the CSV byte for byte with ROS2Logger's when `ros2_logger` is importable.

The real gains come from the native API, as `docs/MIGRATION.md` explains step by step:

| ROS2Logger habit | native flight_recorder |
|---|---|
| one `LogType` per variable, all in one wide table | one **stream** per rate or producer |
| re-logging slices of an array every tick | **record** the array once when it changes; log its id per tick |
| strings in logs | **events** |
| parameters hard-coded in notebooks | **metadata** in the file (`git_commit()`) |
| write at shutdown only | `autosave_period=` (Python) or a periodic `flush()` (C++) |

: Migration, conceptually. {#tbl-migration tbl-colwidths="[50,50]"}

Notebooks that expect the old CSV can be fed from the new files with
`flight_recorder ros2logger-csv run.h5 ticks -o run.csv`.

# Benchmarks {#sec-bench}

`benchmarks/bench_logging.py` flies the same synthetic 5-minute, 100 Hz flight through eight logging methods:
30 000 ticks × 20 float64 values, plus a new 100 × 10 plan every 50 ticks, every plan different so compression gets
no free wins. Each method runs in **its own fresh Python process**, twice: once for timing and once for memory,
because allocation tracing (`tracemalloc`) slows every allocation. The `noop` method measures the harness itself.
The numbers below are from `benchmarks/results_python.md` (Python 3.12.3, NumPy 1.26, h5py 3.16, pandas 3.0,
14-core desktop in performance mode).

![The recorded benchmark results. Memory and full-GC pause are shown after subtracting the harness (`noop`: 5.1 MB,
10.0 ms). The red ticks on the first panel mark p99.](figures/benchmarks.pdf){#fig-bench width=100%}

| method | append p50 / p99 [µs] | memory [MB] | GC-tracked | save [ms] | file [MB] | read [ms] |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ROS2Logger (`LogType` lists → CSV) | 1.68 / 86.3 | 42.4 | 60 000 | 1281 | 26.0 | 151 |
| list of rows → CSV | 1.36 / 23.3 | 45.1 | 90 600 | 305 | 11.8 | 67 |
| list of dicts → pandas → CSV | 2.11 / 6.3 | 33.4 | 0 | 402 | 11.8 | 67 |
| NumPy preallocated → `savez_compressed` | 0.34 / 3.3 | 9.6 | 0 | 243 | 9.2 | 23 |
| pickle of tuples | 1.75 / 5.6 | 25.5 | 690 | 15 | 10.3 | 51 |
| rclpy publish per tick (→ rosbag2) | 4.18 / 31.9 | 4.5 | 0 | – | – | – |
| **flight_recorder (Python)** | **0.52 / 1.6** | **5.1** | **600** | 246 | 11.3 | **17** |
| **flight_recorder (C++)** | **0.015 / 2.3** | 4.8 (buffer) | – | 158 | 11.3 | – |

: Benchmark summary. Memory is after subtracting the harness; rclpy publishing is saved by another process (rosbag2). {#tbl-bench tbl-colwidths="[31,15,11,11,10,11,11]"}

How to read it:

* **Append.** flight_recorder is as cheap as a raw preallocated NumPy row write, and its p99 is the lowest of all
  (1.6 µs). The long tails of the list-based methods (23–86 µs) are allocation and GC work landing inside the loop.
* **Memory and GC.** ROS2Logger holds 42 MB for 4.8 MB of numbers, and lists of rows add 90 600 tracked objects.
  flight_recorder's 600 tracked objects are one small entry per stored plan. The recorder keeps every record
  (with its arrays) for its whole lifetime (section [-@sec-limitations]).
* **Full-GC pause.** The column is one full collection at the end of a small benchmark process. What matters is the
  difference from the harness: +19 ms for ROS2Logger, +16 ms for lists, and nothing for flight_recorder. In a real
  node the whole heap is scanned, so the absolute pauses are far larger (≈300 ms in the RTA node).
* **File size.** Random test data does not compress, so the per-tick sizes are close to each other here. On a real
  flight the per-tick table is 0.36 MB in flight_recorder against 1.28 MB as CSV. The whole ROS2Logger-layout CSV of
  that flight was 5.42 MB, while flight_recorder stored it *plus* every full plan in 1.61 MB.
* **Read back.** 17 ms, because loading is decompression plus float64 arrays: no text parsing.

To reproduce: `python3 benchmarks/bench_logging.py --out results.md` (methods whose dependency is missing, e.g.
`ros2_logger`, are reported as skipped). For C++: `cpp_bench out.h5` prints the append percentiles and the save time
as JSON.

: The 31 test cases. {#tbl-tests tbl-colwidths="[45,55]"}

With colcon, `colcon test --packages-select flight_recorder && colcon test-result --verbose`. The CMake test
registration passes `CPP_EXAMPLE`, `CPP_EDGE_CASES` and `PYTHONPATH` for you. Without colcon:

```bash
g++ -O2 -std=c++17 -Iinclude -I/usr/include/hdf5/serial examples/cpp_example.cpp \
    -L/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/hdf5/serial -lhdf5 -pthread -o /tmp/cpp_example
CPP_EXAMPLE=/tmp/cpp_example PYTHONPATH=. python3 -m pytest -q test
```

When this guide was built (v0.1.2): **30 passed, 1 skipped** (the byte-identical ROS2Logger comparison, because

concurrent flush thread, ThreadSanitizer: no findings.

# Limitations, gotchas and FAQ {#sec-limitations}

## By design

* **Streams are float64 only.** Integers and booleans are exact up to 2^53^. Strings go in events or metadata,
  arrays in records.
* **Columns are fixed per stream.** To log something new, declare another stream.
* **Not a middleware recorder.** Use rosbag2 for topics.
* **One writer process per file.** Different nodes should use different files.
* **A crash during a flush can corrupt the file** (section [-@sec-flush]).

## Behaviours to know about

* `record()` keeps its arrays **by reference** (unless `copy=True`). Modifying a plan array in place before the
  next flush changes what gets written.
* Records and events are held in memory only **until they are flushed**, then released (both writers). Between
  flushes they accumulate, so don't use `record()` as a per-tick stream.
* Re-recording a key deletes and rewrites its HDF5 group. HDF5 does not reclaim the freed space, so re-recording
  large arrays many times makes the file grow; `h5repack` compacts it.
* The first flush truncates an existing file at the same path (a recorder starts a new flight).
* Array and attribute names of one record share a namespace: a clash raises at `record()`. For files written by
  0.1.1 or earlier, `FlightLog.record` keeps the array, warns, and `record_attrs()` returns the attributes.

Fixed in 0.1.2: a single value passed to a multi-column `append` was silently broadcast over all columns;
`start_autosave` after `save()` started a thread that exited at once; flushed records and events stayed in memory;
concurrent `set_metadata` and flush were unsynchronised; the reader ignored `format_version`; Python replaced any
extension with `.h5`; C++ disabled HDF5 error printing process-wide, had no destructor flush, could not write scalar
arrays, and did not check `Array` size against shape (an out-of-bounds read).

## FAQ

**How large should `capacity` be?** About the number of rows in the flight: rate × duration. It is only a
performance hint in Python (doubling beyond it) and in C++ (one block allocation every 4096 rows beyond it).

**Can I read the file during the flight?** Yes, between flushes. The file is closed and consistent then, and
`FlightLog` opens it read-only.

**How do I log a boolean or a mode?** As a float column (`1.0`/`0.0`, or a mode index). For a textual transition,
also log an event.

**Different rates?** Use one stream per rate and join them with `pd.merge_asof(..., on='time')`.

**I need Parquet / MATLAB / CSV.** `log['ticks'].to_parquet(...)`; MATLAB and Julia read the HDF5 directly; the CLI
writes CSV.

**How much data is lost in a crash?** At most one autosave period (Python) or one flush interval (C++). The in-memory
buffer since the last flush is lost; everything before it is on disk.

# Reproducing this guide

```bash
cd docs/guide
python3 make_figures.py           # needs numpy, h5py, pandas, matplotlib; ~1 min
quarto render flight_recorder_guide.qmd
```

`make_figures.py` writes every figure as PDF with TrueType (Type 42) fonts, never Type 3, plus the Markdown snippets
included above: the real file tree, the `summary()` output and the measured hot-path table. The hot-path table and
[@fig-latency] are re-measured on every build, so they vary with the machine; the benchmark figure and table come from
`benchmarks/results_python.md`.
